title: Philosophers Behaving Oddly
description: Diogenes in his jar, Wittgenstein's poker, and the seamstress Schopenhauer paid for life

concepts.title: The Man in the Jar
concepts.contentHtml:
Diogenes of Sinope wanted a cottage in Athens and asked a friend to find him one. The friend was slow about it, so the philosopher moved into the big jar at the Metroön instead, or so says his biographer Diogenes Laertius, who adds that Diogenes explained the move in his own letters.1 The Greek word for that jar is pithos: a large wine jar, usually made of earthenware.2 The barrel he is so often pictured in today is a translation slip. Older translators who met the Latin word dolium did not know exactly what it meant and wrote barrel.3

The most famous scene is set in Corinth. In Plutarch's version, Alexander the Great came to find Diogenes, who was lying in the sun in a suburb called the Cranium. When the king kindly asked if he wanted anything, Diogenes replied, in one old translation, "I would have you stand from between me and the sun." As Alexander walked away, his followers were laughing at the surly philosopher, but he told them that if he were not Alexander, he would choose to be Diogenes.4

Diogenes was also said to have carried a lit lamp through the streets in broad daylight, explaining that he was searching for a human being. How much of this really happened? Nobody can say. These are anecdotes, retold and polished for centuries, and his life and his legend are tightly interwoven. Scholars are sure of one thing: the coinage scandal that drove him from Sinope, because the coins themselves bear it out. It is even disputed whether Diogenes wrote anything at all, which leaves those letters about the jar on shaky ground. Still, the stories make his point. For a Cynic, the way you lived was the argument.5

concepts.title: Wittgenstein's Poker
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2020 the archive of King's College, Cambridge, took in an account of a fireplace poker found in a college room. It is believed to be the very poker that Ludwig Wittgenstein brandished at Karl Popper on 25 October 1946, at a meeting of the Moral Sciences Club in Richard Braithwaite's room at King's.1

Popper had come to read a paper titled "Are There Philosophical Problems?" He argued that there were. Wittgenstein believed there were not: philosophy, for him, dealt in linguistic puzzles, not real problems. For ten minutes the two men jousted, while Wittgenstein grabbed the poker and waved it. In Popper's account, Wittgenstein demanded an example of a moral rule, Popper replied "Not to threaten visiting lecturers with pokers," and Wittgenstein dropped the poker and stormed out. It is a perfect story, and that is the trouble. Decades later, letters in the Times Literary Supplement charged that Popper had distorted the evening to make himself the victor. Two journalists, David Edmonds and John Eidinow, set out to settle it, interviewing surviving witnesses such as the philosophers Peter Geach and Stephen Toulmin.2

Their book, Wittgenstein's Poker (2001), accepts part of the story: Wittgenstein was gesturing with the poker, he did leave early, and he did shut the door noisily behind him. But the authors conclude that the order of events Popper gave is spurious. He published his version in his autobiography in 1974, 23 years after Wittgenstein's death, and the evidence does not support the picture of Wittgenstein storming out in a fury after being bested. Why would Popper tell it that way? The authors point to his growing resentment of a rival who seemed to have every advantage of birth, connections and academic regard, while Popper felt he had never won the recognition he deserved.3

concepts.title: Schopenhauer and the Seamstress
concepts.contentHtml:
Berlin, 1821. Arthur Schopenhauer came home to find three women chatting in the small entrance hall he shared with another lodger, and demanded that they leave. Two did. The third, a seamstress who lodged in the same house, refused. Schopenhauer, stick in hand, threw her out of the house by force, twice, and she fell. The next day she took him to court. He won the first round, but on appeal, heard while he was away, he was fined, and she then sued again, claiming her injuries had left her unable to work.1

Her name was Caroline Marquet, and she said the philosopher had beaten and kicked her. Schopenhauer lost. The court ordered him to pay her 60 thalers a year for the rest of her life.2 The case dragged on for years: an interim ruling by the Berlin appeal court, dated 4 May 1827, still survives among his papers in Frankfurt.3

She lived about twenty more years. When she died, Schopenhauer wrote a Latin pun on her death certificate: Obit anus, abit onus, "the old woman dies, the burden departs." The story comes from his biographer Wilhelm von Gwinner, who dates it to 1841. Even the joke was secondhand. It appears in Sulzer's Theory of the Fine Arts, a reference book Schopenhauer used heavily, where friends at dinner make anagrams of the name of a Hungarian preacher, Tobianus, who had recently lost a wife and gained her fortune. Obit anus, says one guest; Abit onus, says the next.4

title: Strange Deaths and Legends
description: Empedocles and Etna's bronze slipper, Chrysippus laughing at a donkey, Bacon's frozen hen

concepts.title: Empedocles and the Bronze Slipper
concepts.contentHtml:
Mount Etna, Sicily, in the fifth century BC. According to a writer named Hippobotus, the philosopher Empedocles of Acragas walked up to the volcano and plunged into its fiery craters, so that he would simply vanish and confirm the report that he had become a god. The truth came out when the volcano threw up one of his slippers: Empedocles always wore slippers of bronze. He had, after all, greeted his fellow citizens in verse with the words "I go about among you an immortal god, no more a mortal."1

The biographer who preserved this, Diogenes Laertius, did not vouch for it. He piled up rival versions. The historian Timaeus insisted that Empedocles left Sicily for the Peloponnese and never came back, which is why nobody knew how he died, and he dismissed one teller of the god story, Heraclides, as "just such a collector of absurdities." Others said Empedocles fell from a carriage and broke his thigh, hanged himself from a tree, or slipped into the sea in old age and drowned. Diogenes Laertius even wrote a mocking epigram: if he leapt into the fire, how was his tomb still shown in Megara?2

The leap won anyway, because it was the better story. The Roman poet Horace told how Empedocles, wanting to be thought an immortal god, coolly jumped into burning Etna.3 Modern scholars are firmer than any ancient writer. Empedocles was a serious thinker, the source of the four roots, air, water, earth and fire, moved by Love and Strife. But his ancient biography, written some seven centuries after him, is largely a romantic confection, partly spun from his own boastful poems. As the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts it, we can be sure he did not make the fiery leap. He may have died in the Peloponnese, but that is all anyone can say.4

concepts.title: Death by Laughter
concepts.contentHtml:
Chrysippus of Soli (c. 280–207 BC) was the most influential of the early Stoics. He succeeded Cleanthes as head of the school, and he is reported to have written more than 705 books, of which not a single one survives whole. A later Stoic catchphrase held that without Chrysippus there would have been no Stoa at all.1

Yet his most famous moment is his exit. The biographer Diogenes Laertius gives two versions. In the first, taken from Hermippus, Chrysippus was at a sacrificial feast with his pupils, drank a draught of sweet wine unmixed with water, grew dizzy and died five days later, aged 73. In the second, a donkey ate his figs. Chrysippus cried out to the old woman of the house, "Now give the ass a drink of pure wine to wash down the figs," and then laughed so heartily that he died.2

Should anyone believe the second? It has the look of a wandering anecdote. Lucian tells almost exactly the same tale about Philemon, a comic poet said to have lived to 97: lying on his couch, he saw a donkey eating the figs set out for him, burst out laughing, told his servant to give the donkey a sup of wine as well, and choked with laughter.3 The Byzantine encyclopedia called the Suda also says Philemon died of violent laughter, and its modern translators list Chrysippus as another famous victim of the same fate.4 A good joke about a donkey with expensive tastes seems to have drifted between famous old men. Diogenes Laertius, at least, tells the duller wine story first.

concepts.title: Francis Bacon's Frozen Hen
concepts.contentHtml:
Francis Bacon, philosopher and once Lord Chancellor of England, was taking the air in a coach toward Highgate with the king's physician. Snow lay on the ground, and Bacon began to wonder why flesh might not be preserved in snow, as in salt. The two men got out at a poor woman's house at the bottom of Highgate Hill, bought a hen, had her gut it, and stuffed it with snow, Bacon helping with his own hands. The cold chilled him so badly that he could not get home. He went instead to the Earl of Arundel's house nearby, where he was put into a damp bed nobody had slept in for about a year, and within two or three days he was dead.

That is the famous version, set down by John Aubrey in his Brief Lives. Aubrey was not there. He was born only weeks before Bacon died, and he says he had the story from Thomas Hobbes, who used to walk with Bacon and write down his ideas as they came to him.1

Bacon left his own account. Too ill to hold a pen steadily, he dictated a letter to Arundel, the last he ever wrote. He compared himself to Pliny the Elder, who died investigating Vesuvius, and said he had been trying an experiment or two touching the "conservation and induration of bodies", that is, preserving and hardening them. "As for the experiment itself, it succeeded excellently well," he wrote, but on the road he had been taken so ill that he could not tell whether it was the stone, a surfeit or a cold. The letter mentions no snow and no hen. He died on 9 April 1626, Easter Sunday. His Victorian editor James Spedding accepted the snow, an unseasonable late-March fall, and judged the illness to be bronchitis.2

Others doubt the whole tale. John Gribbin, in his book The Fellowship, sets out in detail why he believes the frozen hen story is untrue.3 The legend even has a sequel: tales of a ghostly chicken haunting Pond Square in Highgate, which one Nature blogger dismissed as pure cock and bull.4

title: Philosophers Meet the Real World
description: Thales and the olive presses, the legend of Kant's walk, and Hobbes's war on the circle

concepts.title: Thales: Tycoon or Stargazer?
concepts.contentHtml:
Two of the oldest stories about Thales of Miletus point in opposite directions. In Aristotle's version, people taunted Thales for his poverty, as if it proved that philosophy was useless. So while it was still winter he used his knowledge of the stars to foresee a big olive crop, paid small deposits on every olive press in Miletus and Chios, and when the harvest came, rented them out on his own terms. He made a fortune, proving, Aristotle says, that philosophers could easily be rich if they chose, but that this is not what they care about. Aristotle tells it as hearsay ("so the story goes") and adds that the trick is really just a monopoly, which any business can use.1

Plato tells the opposite tale. Thales was studying the stars, looking upward, when he fell into a pit, and a witty Thracian servant girl, they say, jeered that he was so eager to know the things in the sky that he could not see what was at his feet. Plato's Socrates adds that the same jest applies to everyone who spends a life in philosophy.2 In a later retelling by Diogenes Laertius, the girl has become an old woman who took Thales outdoors to watch the stars, and the pit has become a ditch.3

Neither story is good evidence. None of Thales's writing survives, if he wrote anything at all, and ancient authors had a habit of crediting famous men with things they never did. As one historian put it, the fall may be the first absent-minded professor joke in the West.4 The classicist James Longrigg points out that Aristotle himself disbelieved the olive story, and that the two tales come from separate traditions: one paints the philosopher as a practical man of affairs, the other as an unworldly dreamer. Still, he suspects a grain of truth in the fall, since it is odd to pin it on a man so famously practical.5

concepts.title: Setting Your Watch by Kant
concepts.contentHtml:
The one thing many people know about Immanuel Kant's life is that it ran like a clock. In the famous version, his afternoon walk was so regular that the citizens of Königsberg set their watches by it: "the neighbours knew that it was exactly half past three when Immanuel Kant, in his grey frock coat, rattan cane in hand, emerged from his front door." That line traces back to an essay by the poet Heinrich Heine, who was no eyewitness and had never even met Kant. The Kant of the biographies is less mechanical: he played billiards, gambled and socialized with the great and good of Königsberg.1

Heine's essay, first published in French in 1834, also says the cathedral clock did its work no more regularly than Kant, and that on gloomy days his old servant Lampe plodded after him with an umbrella, "like a symbol of Providence". In an 1887 English translation, though, the neighbors know it is half past four.2 Even the legend cannot settle the hour.

The people who knew him tell a looser story. In Kant's later years, his former secretary Wasianski recorded, dinner with friends ran from one o'clock to four, five or even later, and only then did Kant go out to walk. He went alone, partly because he wanted to breathe only through his nose, which he believed kept off coughs and colds.3 A walk that waits for a long lunch to end is a poor way to set a watch.

The other famous detail, that Kant missed his walk only once, when he was reading Rousseau, is also legend. What is solid is his admiration: a portrait of Rousseau was the only image on display in his house.4 Even the legend comes in versions. One says that Emile (1762), Rousseau's book on education, so captivated Kant that he missed his walk for several days.5

concepts.title: Hobbes Squares the Circle (He Thought)
concepts.contentHtml:
Thomas Hobbes, author of Leviathan, came to mathematics late and, by his friend John Aubrey's account, by accident. He was forty when he found Euclid's Elements lying open in a gentleman's library at the 47th proposition of the first book. "By God," he said, "this is impossible!" He traced the proof back step by step until convinced, and fell in love with geometry. (Aubrey liked a good story, and this one may be polished.) In De Corpore (1655) Hobbes announced that he had squared the circle: built, with ruler and compass alone, a square with exactly the area of a given circle. Friends spotted errors before the book was finished, so Hobbes hedged, telling readers to take his results "problematically". He mocked the new algebra as a scab of symbols, "as if a hen had been scraping there".1

The man who took his proofs apart was John Wallis, Oxford's Savilian Professor of Geometry, a former codebreaker for Parliament and the first to use the symbol ∞. The pamphlets flew, from Wallis's Due Correction for Mr Hobbes, or School Discipline for not saying his Lessons Aright to Hobbes's The Marks of the Absurd Geometry, Rural Language etc. of Doctor Wallis. Hobbes wrote that "either I alone am mad, or I alone am not mad." Wallis answered that if Hobbes was mad, "he is not likely to be convinced by reason". The quarrel ran for more than 20 years and ended only with Hobbes's death.2

Why so much heat over a geometry problem? The historian Douglas Jesseph argues that Hobbes hoped his materialist geometry would vindicate his whole philosophy, while Wallis, a Presbyterian divine as well as a mathematician, attacked the geometry to discredit a philosophy he saw as atheism mixed with dangerous politics.3 Hobbes (1588–1679) is still best remembered in mathematics for his repeated unsuccessful attempts to square the circle.4 They could never have worked. In 1882 Ferdinand von Lindemann proved that pi is transcendental, which makes the construction impossible.5

title: Thought Experiments Gone Wild
description: Buridan's starving donkey, Molyneux's blind man given sight, and Newcomb's two boxes

concepts.title: Buridan's Ass Was Never Buridan's
concepts.contentHtml:
A hungry donkey stands exactly halfway between two equally tempting piles of hay. With no reason to prefer either, it never moves, and starves. This is Buridan's ass, named for John Buridan, perhaps the most influential Paris philosopher of the 14th century, but the donkey appears nowhere in his writings. Most likely his critics invented it as a parody. Buridan held that the will's freedom includes the power to put off a choice, sending an uncertain judgment back for more thought. His opponents found it absurd that freedom could consist in doing nothing, which leaves the donkey free, but dead.1

The puzzle itself is much older. Aristotle, rejecting the idea that the earth stays at the center of the cosmos simply because it has no reason to move one way rather than another, compared it to a man who, "though exceedingly hungry and thirsty, and both equally, yet being equidistant from food and drink, is therefore bound to stay where he is".2 Spinoza took the case seriously in his Ethics. He admitted that a man in such perfect balance would die of hunger and thirst. Asked whether such a man should be considered an ass rather than a man, he replied: "I do not know."3

Then the donkey turned up inside computers. In 1984 the computer scientist Leslie Lamport stated Buridan's principle: a discrete decision based on an input that can vary continuously cannot always be made within a fixed time. Engineers call it the arbiter problem: a computer deciding whether a device's signal arrived in time can be caught halfway, with a wire at a voltage that reads as neither 0 nor 1. Designers allow enough time that this is far rarer than other failures.4 When Lamport sent the paper to Science, one reviewer wrote, "This may be an elaborate joke." It was rejected, and appeared in Foundations of Physics only in 2012.5

concepts.title: Molyneux's Question: Seeing What You Felt
concepts.contentHtml:
The Irish scientist William Molyneux had a personal reason to think about blindness: his wife lost her sight in the first year of their marriage. On 7 July 1688 he wrote to John Locke with a puzzle. Suppose a man born blind has learned to tell a globe from a cube by touch. Given sight, could he tell which was which just by looking? For reasons unknown, Locke never replied. Molyneux tried again in 1693, and this time Locke printed the problem in the second edition of his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1694).

Molyneux answered no: the man knows how a cube feels, not how it looks. Locke agreed that the blind man, "at first sight, would not be able with certainty to say, which was the Globe, which the Cube". Leibniz answered yes, but wanted time allowed for the newly opened eyes to recover. A clean test was hard, because few real patients fit Molyneux's profile: most blindness from birth is treated in infancy.1

In 2011 a team including MIT's Pawan Sinha and Richard Held tested five patients, aged 8 to 17 and all born blind, through Project Prakash, which restores sight to blind children in India. After surgery they could match one seen object to another with more than 90 percent accuracy, and one felt object to another by touch. But asked to pick out by sight an object they had only handled, they did not do much better than if they had guessed.2 The paper's title gave Locke's verdict: "The newly sighted fail to match seen with felt." Yet the link formed fast, within days of surgery.3

Other animals may start with the link in place. In 2024 a team at Queen Mary University of London raised newly hatched chicks in darkness, each with a smooth or a bumpy object to touch for its first 24 hours. On first seeing light, chicks that had touched the smooth object preferred to approach a smooth one, and the bumpy group a bumpy one.4

concepts.title: Newcomb's Two Boxes
concepts.contentHtml:
Imagine a being whose predictions about your choices have never, as far as you know, been wrong. In front of you are two boxes. The first is transparent and holds $1,000. The second is opaque: the being has put $1 million in it if it predicted you would take only that box, and nothing if it predicted you would take both. The prediction was made, and the boxes filled, before you walked in. Do you take one box or two? The puzzle was devised by a physicist, William Newcomb, of the Livermore Radiation Laboratories in California, and the philosopher Robert Nozick made it famous in a 1969 essay. "It is a beautiful problem," Nozick wrote. "I wish it were mine." He put it to friends and students, and found that almost everyone thought the answer was perfectly clear. The trouble was that they divided almost evenly, "with large numbers thinking that the opposing half is just being silly".1

Each side has a respectable principle. One-boxers follow expected utility: because the prediction is reliable, taking one box almost always comes with the million, and taking both almost always comes with just $1,000. Two-boxers follow dominance: the money is already there or it is not, and either way, taking both boxes gets you $1,000 more. Two rules that usually agree give opposite answers. Nor is the puzzle pure fantasy: in "medical" versions, a habit and an illness are correlated only because both have a common cause.2

Philosophers still disagree. In the 2020 PhilPapers Survey, of 1,071 philosophers familiar enough to answer, 39.03% accepted or leaned toward two boxes, 31.19% toward one box, and 30.81% gave some other answer.3 The public leans the other way. When the Guardian ran an online poll in 2016, it counted 31,854 votes: 53.5% took the opaque box alone and 46.5% took both.4
